- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecast is flat or rising slowly, expect overshoot or overconfidence; adjust downward by 2–5% if true outcome shows sharp drop or volatility spike.
- If official event net supply is negative and sentiment is bearish, model tends to underreact — increase forecast baseline by 3–8% to compensate for suppressed volatility.
- After a sharp spike in price (true outcome > 85), model often overestimates continuation — reduce forecast slope by 0.5–1.5 units per day for next 3–5 days.
- When sentiment history shows repeated negative spikes (e.g., -0.33, 0.00), model tends to ignore them — apply a “sentiment decay” filter: if sentiment < 0.33 for 3+ consecutive days, reduce forecast by 1–3% per day.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, mean reversion bias is common — if forecast is > 85 and true outcome drops below 80, apply a “reversion penalty” of 1–3% per day until price stabilizes.
- If official events show high bullish count but supply net is negative, model often overestimates upside — cap forecast at 85–90% of historical max for 3–5 days.
- When sentiment is mixed (0.33–0.67) and events are neutral, model tends to drift toward historical mean — use a “sentiment-weighted mean” correction: blend forecast with 50% historical 18-day average if sentiment < 0.50.
